Note that the length of the altitude (height) can be related to the area of the triangle as follows:

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},
$$

 
where $b$ is a base and $h$ is the corresponding altitude of the triangle.

For the $\bigtriangleup\!ABC,$ we have $h=CH,$ and $b=AB.$ So, we have

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{1}{2} CH \cdot AB.
$$

So, to find $CH,$ we first find $A_{\bigtriangleup}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,0,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0\cdot 1-2\cdot (-2))\mathbf{i}-(2\cdot 1-2\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+(2\cdot (-2)-0\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =4\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC}| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $\bigtriangleup\!ABC$ is

$$
A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{1}{2}A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 6 = 3.
$$

Let's also compute $AB$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =|\overset{\to }{AB}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula $A_{\bigtriangleup} = \dfrac{1}{2} CH \cdot AB,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot AB \\ 3 & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot 2\sqrt{2} \\ 3 & =CH\cdot \sqrt{2} \\ CH & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ CH & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,1,-3)$ to $(-1,2,-2).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-\,\mathbf{i}+2\,\mathbf{j}-2\,\mathbf{k}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =(\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k})+t[(-\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k})] \\  & =(\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k})+t(-\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(t-3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-t, y=t+1,$ and $z=t-3$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z) = x^2+y-z$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(-t)^{2}+(t+1)-(t-3) \\  & ={t}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We notice the following:

- Each vector in our vector field is parallel to the $x$-axis. So, the $\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ components of our vector field are zero everywhere. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
K(x,y,z)=-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}
$$

- Moreover, each vector in our vector field is pointing in the *negative* $x$-direction, so the $\mathbf{i}$ component of our vector field is negative. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
F(x,y,z)=\mathbf{i}
$$

- Finally, we note that each vector in our vector field has the same length, so the $\mathbf{i}$ component of our vector field is constant. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
G(x,y,z)=-y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $\mathbf{H}(x,y,z)=-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}.$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=z-3y,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Δ} & =\{(x,y,z)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\hspace{0.222em}0\le w\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-3-0) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(x+z)\operatorname{cos}(z-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}V & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(u+v)\operatorname{cos}v\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(u+v)\operatorname{cos}v\cdot |-\frac{1}{3}|\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\color{blue}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{1}{3}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(u+v)\operatorname{cos}v\hspace{0.167em}}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}w\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}u\end{aligned}
$$
